The main methodological point is that we are not asking which modern elements can be detected in ancient materials; we are asking which elements had a recognized place in the poem’s elemental material vocabulary. That is why the zinc/antimony caveat matters. Charcoal, soot, and ἄνθρακες may be carbonaceous in modern terms, but they are not treated as a distinct elemental substance alongside gold, silver, copper/bronze, iron, or sulfur. If we counted carbon through every fuel residue, we would be retrojecting modern chemistry and would blur the very distinction the question is drawing.

Sulfur should stay out of the absent list because it is named in the Book 22 purification. Iron is marginal but textually present in the Cyclops passage, so it is not a clean absence. Tin remains the clearest case: bronze is consistently χάλκος, and the tin component is never isolated as κάσσιτερος, which is post-Homeric. Mercury/quicksilver is simply never named or described. Lead is the conventional third on a strict Odyssey-only, free-element-name reading; the μόλυβδος material that can be adduced is not a secure part of the Odyssey’s own elemental name-stock. So I would keep the answer at **Pb, Sn, Hg**—lead, tin, and mercury—rather than adding carbon.

8.text:
The Odyssey’s material name-stock is the Bronze-Age native metal stock with the two later additions that the text actually makes.

* chrysos χρυσός Au gold, argyros ἄργυρος Ag silver and chalkos χαλκός = the working copper/bronze Cu are recurrent and uncontroversial.
* theion θεῖον S is the fumigant of the post-slaughter purification Od. 22.478-481, so sulphur is named in the Odyssey proper.
* sideros σίδηρος Fe is in the Odyssey text, Od. 9.390-393 in the Polyphemos anecdote. It is a hapax/late gloss but it is a naming of iron in the poem.

Zn and Sb are excluded by the terms of the question and carbon is not a Homeric elemental category. ἄνθρακες charcoal/soot are carbonaceous fuel residues, not a distinct elemental substance in the ancient inventory; counting carbon would be the modern chemical retrojection that the Zn/Sb caveat is meant to block.

On the classical seven workable native metals available in the 8th–7th c. E. Mediterranean

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

with native S, the Odyssey gives a distinct elemental name to Au, Ag, Cu/chalkos, marginally Fe and S.

The three classical metals that never receive a separate Homeric elemental name in the Odyssey proper are therefore

* Sn tin. Bronze is always chalkos. The Greek technical name for metallic tin kassiteros κάσσιτερος is post-Homeric. Tin is present only as the unanalysed alloying component of chalkos/bronze and is never isolated and named as a separate element.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος / hydrargos is post-Homeric. The naturally liquid metal is known in the Near East in the period but it is never named or described in Homeric diction.
* Pb lead. On a strict Odyssey-only, pure-element-name criterion μόλυβδος has no secure, recurrent free-elemental attestation in the Odyssey proper. The references usually adduced are Iliadic, scholiastic or later editorial. In the normal textbook formulation Pb is therefore placed with Sn and Hg as the classical metal known in elemental form in the Homeric period which is not named as a distinct substance in the Odyssey.

Sn and Hg are the two essentially unanimous lacunae; Pb is the conventional third member on the strict Odyssey-only reading. Au, Ag, Cu/chalkos are named, S is named in Od.22 and Fe is at least nominally named in Od.9, and carbon is not counted as a Homeric element.

11.text:
The Odyssey's material name-stock is the Bronze Age Au/Ag/chalkos stock with the two Homeric text marginalia that are now normally accepted.

* chrysos χρυσός Au gold, argyros ἄργυρος Ag silver and chalkos χαλκός Cu copper/bronze are ubiquitous and uncontroversial.
* sideros σίδηρος Fe is in the text, Od. 9.390-393 in the Polyphemos anecdote, a hapax/late gloss but a naming of iron in the Odyssey diction.
* theion θεῖον S is the fumigant of the post-slaughter purification of the hall, Od. 22.478-482. Sulfur is therefore named in the Odyssey proper.

Carbon in the form of ἄνθρακες charcoal/soot is a carbonaceous fuel residue, not a distinct elemental substance in Homeric terms, and Zn and Sb are excluded by the terms of the question.

On the classical seven native metals workable in the 8th-7th c. E. Mediterranean

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

with native S, the Odyssey gives a distinct elemental name to Au, Ag, Cu/chalkos and, in the conventional reading, to Fe and S.

The elements known in elemental form at the time that never receive a separate Homeric elemental name are:

* Sn tin. Bronze is always chalkos. The Greek technical name for metallic tin kassiteros κάσσιτερος is post-Homeric. Tin is present in the poem only as the unanalysed component of chalkos/bronze and is never isolated and named as a separate element. This is the canonical Homeric lacuna.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος. Hydrargyros is post-Homeric. The naturally liquid metal is known in the Near East in the period but it is never named or described in Homeric diction. Unanimously absent.
* Pb lead μόλυβδος. On a strict Odyssey-only, pure-element-name criterion there is no secure, recurrent molybdos attestation for a free elemental metal in the Odyssey proper. The references adduced are Iliadic, scholiastic or later editorial. On the normal strict name-for-name reading lead is for all practical purposes un-named in the Odyssey material vocabulary and is therefore placed with Sn and Hg as the textbook trio of classical metals absent from the poem.

Sn and Hg are the two absolutely uncontested absences; Pb is the conventional third member on the strict Odyssey text reading. Sulfur is present and carbon is not counted as a Homeric elemental substance.

12.text:
The name-stock that the Odyssey actually uses is the Bronze-Age Au/Ag/Cu stock with the two late ritual additions.

* chrysos χρυσός Au gold, argyros ἄργυρος Ag silver and chalkos χαλκός Cu copper/bronze are recurrent throughout.
* theion θεῖον S is the fumigant of the post-slaughter purification, Od. 22.478-482, so sulfur is named in the Odyssey proper.
* sideros σίδηρος Fe is in the text at Od. 9.390-393 in the Polyphemos anecdote. It is a hapax/late gloss but it is a naming of iron in the Odyssey diction.

Zn and Sb are excluded by stipulation. Carbon is not an elemental category for Homer: ἄνθρακες charcoal/soot are carbonaceous fuel residues, not a recognised distinct elemental substance in the Homeric inventory, and counting it would be the same retrojection the Zn/Sb caveat is designed to block.

On the classical seven native metals workable in the 8th-7th c. East Mediterranean

Au Ag Cu Sn Pb Fe Hg

with native S, the poem names Au, Ag, Cu/chalkos and, in the conventional reading, Fe and S.

The elements known in elemental form at the time that never receive a distinct Homeric elemental name in the Odyssey are

* Sn tin. Bronze is always chalkos. The Greek technical name for metallic tin kassiteros κάσσιτερος is post-Homeric. Tin is present in the poem only as the unanalysed component of chalkos/bronze and is never isolated and named as a separate element. This is the canonical Homeric lacuna.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος/hydrargos is post-Homeric. The naturally liquid metal is known in the Near East in the period but it is never named or described in Iliadic or Odyssean diction.

Pb lead is the conventional third member on a strict Odyssey-only, pure-element-name criterion. Molybdos μόλυβδος has no secure, recurrent free-element attestation as a named material in the Odyssey proper; the references usually adduced are Iliadic, scholiastic or later editorial. On that strict lexical reading lead is for all practical purposes un-named in the Odyssey’s material vocabulary and is normally grouped with Sn and Hg as the textbook Homeric omission.

Hence the undisputed core absent set is Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead joining them as the usual third member on the strict Odyssey text reading. Sulfur is present, iron is at least nominally present, gold/silver/chalkos are ubiquitous, and carbon is not counted as a Homeric element.

I’d keep the absent set at **lead, tin, and mercury**. The one real pressure point is carbon, but I think adding it would break the criterion the question is using. The question asks about elements known/recognized in elemental form, with the zinc/antimony caveat explicitly warning against counting things merely because they were used or because modern chemistry can identify their composition. Charcoal, soot, and ἄνθρακες are carbonaceous materials, but they are not named or classified in the Homeric inventory as the distinct elemental substance carbon alongside gold, silver, copper/bronze, iron, or sulfur. Counting carbon from fuel residue would retroject later chemistry into the poem’s material vocabulary.

The positive name-stock remains gold, silver, copper/chalkos, with iron at least attested in *Odyssey* 9 and sulfur named in the Book 22 purification. On a strict *Odyssey*-only, elemental-name reading, the clean absences are still:

- **Tin**: bronze is χάλκος, but the tin component is never separately named; κάσσιτερος is post-Homeric.
- **Mercury**: never named or described in Homeric diction.
- **Lead**: no secure, recurrent free-elemental naming in the *Odyssey* proper; μόλυβδος material is marginal/editorial.

So **Pb, Sn, Hg** remains the most defensible set, and carbon should not be added.

Charcoal is an impure fuel residue, not a recognized pure element; counting it would require modern chemical analysis, which is exactly what the zinc/antimony caveat warns against. If we counted carbon because charcoal contains it, consistency would push us toward counting tin because bronze contains it—but tin is precisely the classic absence in Homeric diction. Mercury is never named or described, and lead has no secure free-elemental name in the *Odyssey* proper on a strict name-for-name reading. Sulfur is named in Book 22, and iron is at least attested in Book 9, so neither belongs in the absent set. So **Pb, Sn, Hg** remains the most coherent strict *Odyssey*-only answer.
